title: Invisible Influence. How Do Others Shape Our Choices?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Asch, Solomon E., Opinions and Social Pressure, “Scientific American” 193 (1955)
Asch, Solomon E., Studies of Independence and Conformity: I. A Minority of One Against a Unanimous Majority, “Psychological Monographs” 70 (1956)
Bond, Rod; Smith, Peter B., Culture and Conformity: A Meta-Analysis of Studies Using Asch’s (1952b, 1956) Line Judgment Task, “Psychological Bulletin” 119 (1996)
Latané, Bibb; Darley, John M., Group Inhibition of Bystander Intervention in Emergencies, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 10 (1968)

Nolan, Jessica M.; Schultz, P. Wesley; Cialdini, Robert B.; Goldstein, Noah J.; Griskevicius, Vladas, Normative Social Influence Is Underdetected, “Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin” 34 (2008)

paragraphs: A student is filling in a questionnaire in a small waiting room when smoke begins to seep from a ventilation grille. That was the setting of an experiment carried out in New York in the 1960s by the psychologists Bibb Latané and John Darley. When participants sat alone, they usually went quickly to report that something was wrong: three out of four did so. But when two planted men sat with them, shrugging and calmly writing on, only one participant in ten reported the smoke. The rest rubbed their watering eyes and kept filling in the questionnaire, and afterwards insisted that they had judged the situation for themselves.

The influence of others is often strongest where we do not notice it at all. You can see it today in a group of friends where everyone laughs at one person, even though nobody really finds it funny. Yet the same mechanism can also work in the opposite direction. Solomon Asch’s studies of conformity to the majority showed that the presence of even one person who answers differently from the rest can markedly weaken group pressure. Such dissent can give courage to others who also disagree with the majority.

In Antioch, in one of the first Christian communities, believers of Jewish and Gentile background ate together at a shared table. Peter came there, the man who a few years earlier had become convinced that God does not show favoritism (Acts 10:34). He sat down to meals with the Gentile believers, but when men from James’s circle arrived from Jerusalem, he withdrew and began to separate himself from them, “for fear of those in the circumcision group” (Galatians 2:12). He gave in to pressure, and his behavior influenced others. The other Jewish believers followed his example, and in the end so did Barnabas, known for his kindness and open heart. No one had to say outright that the Gentiles were inferior. Simply stepping away from the shared table showed that they were not being treated as equals.

Since no one has earned a place at God’s table, no one has the right to take it away from others either. A community that seats people according to their background contradicts by its behavior what it teaches about God. It may be that today you will be the one person who stays at the table, even as everyone else walks away from it.

Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: At whose table have I stopped sitting because I was afraid of what others would think?
challenge: Before you put down your phone or close your computer today, recall one situation from the past month when you fell silent or changed your mind under the influence of others. Think about whose reaction you were afraid of at the time. Tell God plainly what you feared: laughter, rejection, or perhaps an awkward silence?

paragraphs: New York, the second half of the 1960s. A student at Columbia University is sitting in a small waiting room filling in a questionnaire when whitish smoke begins to seep from a ventilation grille in the wall. At first it is only a thin wisp, then there is more of it, and after a few minutes the whole room is sunk in a gray fog.

The scene had been staged by two American social psychologists, Bibb Latané and John Darley, who wanted to find out how the presence of passive bystanders affects the response to a possible danger. When a participant sat in the waiting room alone, he usually got up, examined the grille and went to report that something was wrong: three out of four did so. In another variant two more men sat beside him, planted by the researchers and instructed not to react, whatever happened. So they glanced at the smoke, shrugged and went back to their questionnaires. The result was striking: in this group only one participant in ten reported the smoke. The others sat in the thickening clouds, coughing, rubbing their watering eyes and dutifully filling in the questionnaire to the end.

When they were later asked why they had not reacted, they explained that they had thought it was probably steam or some fault in the air conditioning. Almost no one admitted to having been guided by the behavior of the others. They were all convinced that they had assessed the situation and made the decision on their own.

Psychologists call this mechanism pluralistic ignorance. A person caught in an unclear situation feels unsure, so they glance at others to see how they are reacting. They see calm faces, because the others are also trying not to betray their unease, and in the end everyone together concludes that nothing is happening. This was confirmed by a third variant of the study, in which the waiting room was occupied by three genuine volunteers: in most of these groups no one reported the smoke. No one persuaded or urged anyone; it was their shared failure to react that led them to the wrong conclusion.

It is this part of the experiment that is most unsettling. The influence of other people is often strongest when we do not notice it. So how can we resist it if we are not even aware that it is acting on us?

Nor is this blindness confined to smoke-filled rooms. Several decades later another experiment was carried out in California. Cards encouraging people to save energy were hung on the doors of homes. Some appealed to concern for the environment, others to social responsibility or to savings on bills. Still others stated, truthfully, that most of the neighbors were trying to save energy. Meter readings showed that in the first weeks the homes that received the message about the neighbors’ behavior used the least electricity. Yet the residents themselves rated that message as the least motivating. Californians had answered in a similar way in a telephone survey before the experiment: they considered the behavior of others the least important of their reasons for saving energy. So the neighbors’ influence showed up in the meter readings, even though the residents themselves attached little importance to it.

sections.heading: Three Lines on a Card
paragraphs: More than a decade before the smoke experiment, the question of how strongly the presence and opinions of others affect our own judgments was explored by Solomon Asch, a Warsaw-born American psychologist whose study became one of the best known in social psychology. A volunteer sat at a table with several other people, and the group was shown a card with a reference line and a second card with three lines for comparison. Each person in turn said aloud which of them was the same length as the reference. The differences between the lines were so obvious that a mistake seemed impossible. The task was very easy: when participants judged the lines on their own, the error rate was below one percent.

What the participants did not know was that the others at the table had been planted. In some rounds they unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer, and the participant answered as one of the last. About three-quarters of participants went along with the group’s wrong answer at least once. In conversations after the experiment only a few claimed that they had really seen the lines differently. Many knew which answer was correct but decided that if everyone else was saying something different, they themselves were probably mistaken. Others simply did not want to stand out from the group.

Although these results are often presented as proof of strong conformity, Asch also drew attention to the opposite: the ability of many people to remain independent. Even when the whole “planted” group unanimously gave the wrong answer, participants still mostly answered correctly, with roughly 2 out of 3 sticking to the right line. And about 1 in 4 participants never once gave in to group pressure, even when everyone around them was saying something wrong.

Particularly interesting was a variant of the study in which one planted participant was instructed to answer correctly. He then became the real participant’s ally and considerably weakened the influence of the rest of the group. In this case participants gave in to the majority four times less often than when they faced it completely alone. So the pressure was strongest as long as the group was unanimous. One dissenting voice was enough for a person to dare to trust their own eyes.

sections.heading: The Table in Antioch
paragraphs: The first generation of Christians went through a very similar situation. In the middle of the first century, Antioch in Syria was one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire. It was there that the first large church arose in which followers of Jesus from Jewish and Gentile families lived side by side, and it was there that the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:19-26). They prayed together and ate together, and in that culture a shared meal was a clear sign of belonging to one community.

Peter came to Antioch, a man who had known Jesus up close. A few years earlier, in Joppa, he had had a vision, after which he went to the house of the Roman centurion Cornelius and there declared: “I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism” (Acts 10:34). Later, in Jerusalem, he had to account for that visit, because he faced the charge: “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them” (Acts 11:3). He defended himself without difficulty then, because he had both the arguments and his own experience on his side.

In Antioch Peter ate with the Gentile believers without any reservations, until men from the circle of James, the brother of Jesus, arrived from Jerusalem. What happened next is described by Paul in his letter to the Galatians: Peter began to draw back from the shared meals and to separate himself from the Gentiles, “for fear of those in the circumcision group” (Galatians 2:12). The Greek verbs here suggest a process spread out over time, so it is easy to imagine how it might have looked. One day Peter sits at a different table; the next he eats earlier, together with the guests from Jerusalem.

The dispute was about the table, not the menu: the question was who sat down to eat with whom. For Christians of Gentile background the message was clear, even though no one said it aloud: “You are a bit inferior.” Words were unnecessary; it was enough that week by week there were more empty places at their table.

Then something happened that Asch would have recognized at once. The other Jewish believers followed Peter, and finally so did Barnabas, one of Paul’s closest co-workers, whom the apostles had once called Son of Encouragement (Acts 4:36). It was he who brought Paul to the apostles when they were all still afraid of him (Acts 9:26-27). It was he who, sent to Antioch, saw God’s grace at work among the Gentiles and sincerely rejoiced (Acts 11:22-23). It is hard to think of a man less open to the suspicion of prejudice. And yet Paul writes that “even Barnabas was led astray” (Galatians 2:13). The Greek word used here literally means “was carried away together with them” and calls to mind someone swept along by the current of a river. Peter himself gave in to pressure, and his behavior began to influence others.

sections.heading: The One Who Stayed at the Table
paragraphs: Paul then did something that took real courage. He told Peter directly, and in front of everyone, that his conduct was out of line with the truth of the gospel that they both preached (Galatians 2:14). He did it publicly because the withdrawal itself had been public. He asked him why he was compelling the Gentiles to live by Jewish customs when he himself, a Jew, lived as they did. Leaving the table was therefore a form of pressure, even though no one had voiced any demand. Paul’s words may have given the Gentile believers a sense that one of the leaders was standing on their side.

It would be easy to turn this scene into a story of a hero and a coward, but the Bible does not allow it. In other letters Paul himself admits to weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9-10), and years later Peter writes of him: “our beloved brother Paul” (2 Peter 3:15). The confrontation did not destroy their bond, and both remained brothers to the end.

This story teaches us several things about ourselves, and the first is the least comfortable. We do not know what the people involved were thinking, but they may have reacted much like the students in the smoky room: if Peter is acting this way, he must know what he is doing. And if Barnabas is sitting elsewhere, that must be the right thing to do. Each of them looked to the others and so confirmed them in their error. If Peter and Barnabas gave in, then group pressure is not a problem only for weak people. It often begins to work when people whose opinion matters to us appear nearby. Sometimes their mere presence is enough; they do not need to demand anything or threaten anyone.

The same mechanism is at work today in far less dramatic circumstances. You can see it in a group of friends where everyone laughs at someone, even though no one really feels like laughing. You can also see it in church, where a newcomer stands alone by the wall after the service because everyone assumes someone else has already gone over to them.

The second lesson is encouraging: pressure falls apart faster than we might think. In Asch’s studies a single ally clearly weakened it, and in Antioch one Paul dared to break the unanimous silence. Perhaps in a similar situation it will be your stance that gives others courage. No speeches are needed for that; sometimes it is enough to stay at the table where others have suddenly stopped sitting.

The third lesson concerns God. In Antioch something more than good manners was at stake. Immediately afterward Paul writes that a person is justified by faith in Jesus Christ, not by works of the law (Galatians 2:16). Since no one has earned a place at God’s table, no one has the right to take it away from others either. A community that seats people according to their background contradicts by its behavior what it teaches about God. It was He who first invited everyone to the table, before anyone had a chance to deserve it.

If in this story you feel closer to Peter than to Paul, you are in good company. After the events in Antioch, God went on leading Peter, teaching him and using him. The first step toward change may look very modest: tell God plainly whose opinion you fear most.

So the influence of others works both ways. Just as shared silence lets smoke fill the whole room, the courage of one person who stands up and says that something is wrong spreads to everyone around. The students in the smoky waiting room needed someone to get up first, and the Gentile believers in Antioch needed someone to stay at their table. Today someone around you may need exactly the same.

questions: At whose table have I stopped sitting because I was afraid of what others would think?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Recall one situation from the past month when you fell silent or changed your mind under the influence of others. Think about whose reaction you were afraid of at the time. Tell God plainly what you feared: laughter, rejection, or perhaps an awkward silence?

**In action.** Today, pay attention to the people around you: at work, at university, after the church service or in a group chat. Think of someone who usually keeps to the sidelines. At a meal, sit next to that person or suggest having a cup of tea together. Ask how their week is going, and listen carefully to the answer. You don’t need to make a big event of it. If you are not meeting anyone in person today, write to someone who may have been left out of a group conversation and ask how they are doing.
